st.headline: ‘Start dating earlier’: Lunch Actually CEO on finding a life partner in S’pore
st.teaser: In polytechnic or university, men and women are on a more similar footing and can grow together, says Violet Lim.
fullText: SINGAPORE – Young people should start dating while they are still in university, instead of waiting until their careers are established to look for a life partner, said Violet Lim, chief executive of regional matchmaking agency Lunch Actually.

At that early stage, men and women are on a more similar footing and can grow together, rather than assess each other against increasingly exacting standards after entering the workforce, she told The Straits Times in an interview.
“Relationships and personal ambitions can develop together.”
Her advice comes as Singapore grapples with fewer marriages, later unions and declining birth rates.

According to the National Population and Talent Division, Singapore’s resident total fertility rate fell to 0.87 in 2025, from 0.97 in 2024. There were 21,671 citizen marriages in 2025, down 5.6 per cent, while the median age at first marriage for citizen grooms and brides rose to 30.8 and 29.1 years, from 30.1 and 27.9 a decade earlier.

While dating apps have made meeting potential partners easier, Lim said increasingly demanding expectations, a desire for certainty and a reluctance to commit are making it harder for singles to build lasting relationships.
She said encouraging relationships earlier is an important part of addressing the problem, as couples must first find each other before they can consider having children.
“Please do not stop your kids from dating when they are in university. Encourage them to date,” Lim said.
Lim noted that more young people view relationships as a distraction from their studies or careers, where hard work offers a clearer “ROI”, or return on investment.

When she speaks at universities and polytechnics, students often tell her they are not dating, with some saying that investing in their career offers better ROI compared with spending years building relationships without a guaranteed outcome.

Some of the traditional reasons for marrying have weakened, as children are no longer seen as necessary to contribute to household income or provide support in old age, Lim added, noting that a rising number of couples are now opting to keep pets instead.

With less parental and societal pressure to settle down, remaining single has become more widely accepted, Lim said. Some also cite longer lifespans as a reason to put off marriage until their 40s or even 50s, rather than spend many decades with the same person.
Meanwhile, among those seeking partners, expectations have become more demanding, with clients now seeking much more information before agreeing to a match.
Physical attraction remains a priority for men, while women increasingly assess how men carry themselves, Lim said, adding that women tend to have higher expectations for a match than men.

Financially independent, well-educated women who enjoy comfortable lifestyles often want partners at a similar or higher level. But the men who match these requirements may have different preferences, narrowing the pool of mutually interested partners, she added.
Some women are also reluctant to consider older men who are further along in their careers, but who may suit the bill.
That is why pairing up at university allows couples to build relationships before differences in professional achievement become a barrier, she said.
Lunch Actually helps compatible and like-minded singles meet through pre-screened, pre-matched and pre-arranged one-to-one dates , alongside offering dating and relationship coaching.
The company claims to have arranged more than 150,000 dates and matched more than 4,500 married couples.

Lim, who started the agency with her husband 22 years ago, noted that the dating environment in Singapore has changed considerably since 2004, when singles often lacked opportunities to meet potential partners.
Today, apps and other platforms offer ample opportunities for folks to meet and date. What is now harder is persuading people to choose a partner and commit.
The way Lim sees it, dates have become more commoditised. “With another potential match readily available, more people wonder whether the next person they meet may be better.”
That "paradox of choice” can produce an endless search, followed by dating fatigue where swiping, chatting and repeatedly making small talk begin to feel like work.

Lim said singles increasingly want certainty before agreeing to a first date, while some spend weeks or months messaging, only to find that the person they eventually meet differs from the image they have built in their minds.
She recommends deciding after about a week of chatting whether to meet, then arranging a date to establish whether there is enough interest to continue.
She urges singles to give an unremarkable first date another chance.
“Many people rule out a second date right after the first. But attraction often develops over several dates, as people take time to discover different sides of each other.”
A first meeting does not need to deliver instant sparks to warrant a second, she said. “A reasonably pleasant encounter can be enough.”
That is where Lunch Actually’s matchmaking and coaching can help, by encouraging clients to examine both their requirements and what they bring to a relationship, said Lim.
She recalled a wealthy, highly educated and accomplished client who wanted to be matched with the top 5% of men in the agency’s database in terms of career and financial success.

cna.headline: Asian markets sell off after US inflation fuels rate hike bets
cna.teaser: Seoul and Tokyo bore the brunt of the selling as traders bailed out of once-imperious chipmakers.
fullText: SINGAPORE: Asian stocks plunged Thursday (Oct 15) as tech firms suffered another painful rout, as a quicker-than-expected increase in US consumer price inflation fuelled expectations the Federal Reserve will have to ramp interest rates higher.
Seoul and Tokyo bore the brunt of the selling as traders bailed out of once-imperious chipmakers, though the selling was heavy across the region, tracking sharp losses on Wall Street.
As of 12.30pm Singapore time, Seoul's Kospi had plunged more than 7 per cent, with SK hynix sinking more than 10 per cent and Samsung more than 10 per cent.
And in Tokyo, the Nikkei 225 shed more than 5 per cent as Kioxia also dived more than 11 per cent and Advantest plunged over 13 per cent. Tech investment titan SoftBank lost more than 9 per cent.

The selling came after many tech firms had clawed back some of the huge losses sustained in a summer rout that came on the back of worries about elevated valuations and questions over when firms would see returns on their colossal investments.
Hong Kong, Shanghai and Jakarta were also in negative territory.
In Singapore, the Straits Times Index fell 0.9 per cent. Chip-testing equipment maker AEM Holdings lost 9 per cent, while UMS Integration dropped 9 per cent and Frencken declined 6.4 per cent.

Markets, already struggling with concerns about the outlook for the AI investment boom, were stung after data showed the US consumer price index hit 3.7 per cent in September, sharply up from the previous month and more than the 3.6 per cent forecast.

The reading is the highest in five months and was largely driven by the surge in energy costs caused by the more than seven-month Iran war, which saw Tehran effectively choke off the Strait of Hormuz, through which a fifth of global crude passed.
Gasoline costs accounted for more than half of the monthly CPI jump, surging 9.1 per cent in September.
All three major American indices dropped overnight but the tech-heavy Nasdaq suffered the deepest declines, losing nearly 2 per cent.

The CPI data lifted expectations of interest rate hikes from the Federal Reserve over the course of the year ahead, possibly as soon as later this month. Fed funds futures are now pricing an implied 31.6 per cent probability of a 25-basis-point hike at the US central bank's next two-day meeting on Oct 28, compared to a 22.1 per cent chance a day earlier, according to the CME Group's FedWatch tool.

"This CPI report is a headache for the Fed, which had been indicating a willingness to pause this month," said Neil Wilson at Saxo Markets, referring to several board members who had suggested they favoured a go-slow approach to assess last month's lift.
"Markets too had all but priced out a hike later this month but repriced for the Fed to move a bit quicker after US inflation came in a little hotter than expected."
